finding: Baseline survey (n=312): 91% had experience of rough sleeping; 27% of these first before 18 and a further 27% at 18-25; 48% had not been in settled housing for five years or more.
quote: prior to entering Housing First, the vast majority (91%) of Clients had experience of rough sleeping

finding: Baseline: 18% had never worked and 72% had not worked in the past year; 52% left school before 16; 54% had any qualification.
quote: one in five (18%) never having worked and a further seven in ten (72%) not having worked in the past year

finding: Baseline: 21% rated health good or very good; 61% longstanding illness or disability; 21% learning disability; 57% registered with a GP.
quote: Six in ten (61%) reported having a longstanding illness or disability, and one in five (21%) reported having a learning disability.

finding: Baseline: 71% took drugs in last three months (crack 41%, heroin/opiates 34%); 33% currently dependent on drugs; of those ever dependent 41% under 16 and 35% at 16-25.
quote: Seven in ten (71%) clients reported taking drugs in the last three months

finding: Baseline: 44% had ASB actions in last six months; 73% had ever been in prison, 16% in the past year; only 26% had not been a victim of crime in the previous six months.
quote: Three quarters (73%) of Clients had spent time in prison, although only 16% had done so in the past year prior to recruitment.

finding: All 81 service users interviewed described long or intermittent periods of homelessness before referral, for most including rough sleeping.
quote: All 81 Housing First service users interviewed across the lifetime of the evaluation described either long or intermittent periods of homelessness

finding: Interviewees described concurrent or serial needs: drugs and/or alcohol, poor physical health, mental health conditions, offending, domestic violence.
quote: Almost without exception interviewees described having a range of needs, typically experienced concurrently or serially rather than singly.

finding: Interviewees described multiple adverse life experiences in childhood and early adulthood (abuse, neglect, abandonment, bereavement, care, gangs, domestic violence, street sex work).
quote: They described a range of adverse life experiences including abuse, neglect, abandonment, the death of parents and close family members

finding: Before entry 86% had precarious living circumstances (31% mostly rough sleeping); at 12 months (n=167) 92% were in long-term accommodation, 87% social renting, none sleeping rough.
quote: A year later, nearly all clients (92%) were living in long-term, largely social rented (87%), accommodation.

finding: 'Often or always' lonely fell from 35% to 16%; 'never' lonely rose from 16% to 27% (p<0.001).
quote: a third (35%) of clients reported ‘often or always’ being lonely, a percentage which had halved to 16% 12 months later

finding: Clients feeling they had someone to listen to them rose from 70% to 81% (p=0.003).
quote: Coming into Housing First, 70% of clients felt they had someone to listen to them, a figure which rose to 81% after a year.

finding: At 12 months 75% felt at home where they lived and 48% reported interaction with people locally (not asked at baseline).
quote: while three quarters (75%) of clients reported feeling at home where they lived, only half (48%) reported interaction with people locally

finding: Feeling safe all of the time rose from 11% to 49% and most of the time from 18% to 22% (p<0.001).
quote: At 12 months, half (49%) of clients felt safe all of the time, with a further fifth (22%) feeling safe most of the time.

finding: Not a victim of crime in the previous six months rose from 30% to 55% (p<0.001).
quote: A year on, 55% reported that they had not been a victim of crime in the preceding six months.

finding: Eating well all of the time rose from 10% to 36%, sleeping well from 3% to 10%; never eating well fell from 22% to 2%, never sleeping well from 42% to 25% (p<0.001).
quote: At baseline, using a five-point scale, 10% of clients reported eating well ‘all of the time’ and 3% slept well ‘all of the time’. A year later, these percentages were 36% and 10%.

finding: Self-rated health very good rose from 4% to 7% and good from 17% to 27% (p=0.002); very bad stayed at 11%.
quote: at baseline, 4% rated their health as ‘very good’ and 17% as ‘good’. A year later, the percentages were 7% and 27%.

finding: Self-reported anxiety fell from 81% to 71% (p=0.014) and depression from 80% to 68% (p=0.009).
quote: significantly fewer reported suffering from anxiety (71% compared to 81% on entering Housing First) and depression (68% compared to 80%)

finding: GP registration rose from 60% to 92% (p<0.001).
quote: a significant increase in the percentage of clients registered with a GP from 60% to 92%

finding: Drug dependency 27% to 25% (p=0.6754) and alcohol dependency 17% to 13% (p=0.117): no significant change.
quote: At baseline, 27% of clients said that they were dependent on drugs, a percentage which was still 25% a year later.

finding: Crack cocaine use fell from 37% to 20% (p<0.001), heroin/opiates from 32% to 21% (p=0.005); drinking monthly or less rose from 14% to 28% (frequency p=0.043).
quote: a fall in the percentage using crack cocaine in the previous three months from 37% before entering Housing First to 20% after a year

finding: Since entering Housing First 51% had received treatment for drug dependency and 17% for alcohol dependency.
quote: Half of clients (51%) had received treatment for drug dependency since entering Housing First, and 17% had done so for alcohol dependency.

finding: ASB involvement fell from 34% to 15%; cautioned, arrested or convicted from 29% to 12% (both p<0.001).
quote: a third (34%) of clients reported having been involved in antisocial behaviour, a figure which dropped to 15% at the 12-month follow-up

finding: At 12 months 4% were in paid work and a further 3% looking for or expecting work.
quote: Only 4% of clients were in paid work and only a further 3% were looking for work or expecting to be in work in the next six months.

finding: Receipt of disability benefits rose from 33% to 56% (p<0.001).
quote: At the 12-month follow-up, 56% of clients were in receipt of disability benefits, compared to 33% before they entered Housing First.

finding: At 12 months 60% said it was completely true they had a desire to succeed and 52% that they had life goals.
quote: six in ten (60%) clients said that it was ‘completely true’ that they had the desire to succeed

finding: Subgroup analysis of 12-month change: no significant variation; indications that older age, earlier first homelessness and cognitive impairment were associated with less progress on health and alcohol/drug dependency; women's accommodation and health outcomes less likely to improve.
quote: showed no significant variation in the extent or nature of outcomes achieved.

finding: Staff report around three years after baseline: 59% still in the programme, 14% graduated, 9% alternative accommodation, 7% died, 3% in prison, 5% lost contact.
quote: Around three years after joining Housing First, six in ten (59%) who provided baseline data when they entered Housing First were still in the programme.

finding: Staff report at three years: 69% of baseline clients alive were in stable accommodation; among those still in Housing First 84% stable, 81% social housing.
quote: Among those still in Housing First, the vast majority (84%) of clients were in stable accommodation around three years after joining Housing First. Most (81%) were in social housing

finding: Only significant three-year subgroup differences in housing: aged 40+ more often in long-term accommodation (76% vs 63%, p=0.040) and still in HF (72% vs 57%); drug dependency at entry less often in long-term accommodation (65% vs 78%, p=0.047).
quote: The only significant sub-group differences in housing status three years after recruitment to Housing First related to age and drug dependency.

finding: Among those still in HF at three years, in previous six months: 57% drug treatment, 31% alcohol, 52% physical health, 42% mental health treatment; 30% attended A&E.
quote: Half (57%) of all clients still in Housing First had received treatment in the previous six months for drug misuse, and a third (31%) had done so for alcohol misuse.

finding: At three years 1% of those still in HF were in (part-time) paid work, 5% volunteering, 2% in education or training.
quote: only 1% of those still on Housing First were in paid work; in all cases this work was part-time

finding: Clients reported as main benefits a tenancy in a chosen area and flexible, non-judgmental support, a platform for other outcomes, including better health support leading to reduced or more stable drug/alcohol intake.
quote: The most frequently reported benefits were being offered the opportunity to accept a tenancy in an area they had chosen and receiving flexible and non-judgmental help from their support worker.

finding: Stakeholders and delivery staff described positive impacts across the outcomes measured in the survey and a large 'distance of travel' for clients.
quote: Stakeholders and delivery staff provided evidence of clients experiencing positive impacts across the full range of outcomes quantitively measured by this evaluation

finding: Interviewees reported benefits not captured by traditional outcome measures (first birthday cake, first GP visit in 35 years, learning to ride a bike).
quote: Significant benefits that could not be captured by traditional outcome measures were also reported.

finding: In client interviews the most frequently reported benefit was being settled in their own property, which gave security and a platform for other outcomes.
quote: In client interviews the most frequently reported benefit, above all others, was being settled in their property and having a space of their own.

finding: Monitoring data at end December 2022: 1,396 accepted over the programme, 884 on the programme (684 housed, 173 waiting, 27 in prison or hospital), 512 exited; 1,061 housed in total.
quote: The total number housed including at end of December 2022 and formerly was 1,061

finding: Exit reasons: loss of contact 103, died 90 (6% of those recruited); graduations 86 (WMCA 67, LCRCA 10, GMHF 9).
quote: the most commonly reported reason for exit was loss of contact with the individual (103), sadly followed by dying while on the programme (90 or 6% of the total number of individuals recruited onto the programme)

finding: 68% had sustained tenancies for one to three years and 10% for over three years; 79% of current clients had sustained tenancies for at least one year.
quote: A total of 79% of current clients had sustained their tenancies for at least one year at the end of December 2022

finding: Housing providers: 67% registered housing providers, 31% council, 2% private rented; council share 57% in WMCA, 13% in GMHF, none in LCRCA.
quote: only 17 (2%) individuals had been accommodated in the private rented sector

finding: GMHF average time from referral to housing fell from 135 days (Year 1) to 94 days (Year 3); in parts of LCRCA waits of up to 47 weeks.
quote: in GMHF the average length of time between referral and housing reduced over the course of the Pilot from 135 days in Year 1 to 94 days in Year 3

finding: All Pilots faced challenges in establishing referral pathways in year one, with inappropriate referrals (without consent, lacking capacity, extremely poor health).
quote: All three Pilots faced challenges in establishing referral pathways and processes across partner agencies in the first year of delivery.

finding: Multi-agency referral panels improved the suitability of referrals and strengthened multi-agency working.
quote: These led to an improvement in the suitability of referrals, helped strengthen multi-agency working and enabled more coherent and joined up packages of support to be delivered.

finding: Securing affordable, suitable accommodation was a major challenge throughout, especially one-bed city centre and adapted properties, worsened by COVID-19 and cost of living.
quote: Securing access to affordable and suitable accommodation has been a major challenge for all three Pilots throughout the lifetime of the programme.

finding: Housing providers' willingness to offer tenancies depended on their perception of HF support; engagement varied; SLAs fell short of pledged properties.
quote: The willingness of providers to offer tenancies is in part contingent upon their perception of the level and longevity of support Housing First is able to provide to tenants.

finding: Tenancy viability depends on practical and emotional support, most intense in the first weeks, later shifting to skills and resilience.
quote: The continuing viability of a tenancy is largely contingent upon the delivery of practical and emotional support to clients once accommodated.

finding: After moving in many clients experience loneliness and isolation, a risk to tenancy security; building social networks and positive activity is key.
quote: After this initial flurry of activity many clients experience feelings of loneliness and social isolation which can pose a risk to tenancy security.

finding: Small caseloads (not exceeding 7) are critical to the intensity of support; where caseloads were exceeded support workers could not deliver it.
quote: The ability to maintain small caseloads (i.e. not exceeding 7) is critical to delivering the quality and consistency of support valued by service users.

finding: Front line staff reported that prompt multi-agency responses, facilitated by good relationships with housing providers, resolved threats to tenancies.
quote: Front line staff reported that prompt multi-agency responses facilitated by existing good relationships between Housing First teams and housing providers can deliver solutions

finding: Clients described relationships with support workers in overwhelmingly positive terms (honesty, trust, empathy, non-conditionality, 'stickability'); delivery teams named perseverance, flexibility and a person-led approach.
quote: In interviews Clients described their relationships with support workers in overwhelmingly positive terms.

finding: Strong consensus among interviewees that most clients need support for indefinite periods because recovery is slow and non-linear; some clients anxious about withdrawal of support.
quote: There was a strong consensus amongst interviewees at both strategic and frontline levels that the majority of clients would need support for indefinite periods of time

finding: Recruitment and retention challenges (pay, short-term contracts, competition, demands of the job); attrition when funding was insecure in late 2021 and early 2022 raised caseloads and stress.
quote: Problems with retention were particularly intense when future funding was insecure towards the end of 2021 and during the first quarter of 2022.

finding: Staff demands were high; reflective practice was offered in all Pilots and, where taken up, was appreciated.
quote: Where these were taken up they were generally much appreciated and described as extremely useful.

finding: Pilots shifted attitudes and working practices; multi-agency panels and MDTs were universally acknowledged to promote person-centred, joined up working.
quote: The development of new, and engagement with existing, multi-agency panels and/or parallel Multi-Disciplinary Teams (MDTs) were universally acknowledged to have promoted person-centred working

finding: Pilots were credited with catalysing 'elastic tolerance' among many housing providers, through relationships and first-hand evidence of effective ways of working.
quote: the Pilots were widely credited as having catalysed the adoption of increasing levels of ‘elastic tolerance’

finding: Drug/alcohol and mental health services improved their understanding, attributed to psychologists and DDPs; inflexibility and thresholds of mental health and drug/alcohol services remained a barrier.
quote: These changes were largely attributed to the input of the psychologists and Dual Diagnosis Practitioners (DDP)

finding: Interviewees saw many adaptations as work-arounds rather than systems change; dissonance between HF flexibility and rigid statutory processes; overstretched services and staff turnover impede change.
quote: many of the procedural adaptations made represented effective ‘work arounds’ rather than the achievement of actual systems change per se.

finding: Understanding of the principles grew but varied; separation of housing and support, and choice and control, poorly understood by some stakeholders.
quote: The separation of housing and support was identified as a principle that is sometimes poorly understood by some stakeholders

finding: Key challenges to fidelity: housing stock, funding uncertainties causing staff shortages and high caseloads, availability of other services (especially mental health), aggravated by COVID-19.
quote: A number of key challenges to delivering on fidelity have been highlighted, including most notably the limited availability of appropriate housing stock, funding uncertainties leading to staff shortages and high caseloads

finding: Internal fidelity self-assessments (GMHF, LCRCA) score highly on separation of housing and support and active engagement.
quote: These score highly on separation of housing and support and the use of an active engagement approach.

finding: Fidelity assessment interviews (72): strengths-based orientation shaped delivery; right to a home and choice and control difficult given housing shortage; harm reduction compromised by access to mental health services.
quote: Delivering on a right to a home and choice and control was described as challenging in the context of a shortage of suitable housing

finding: Total cost to December 2022 £27.96m including in-kind; weighted average annual cost £7,737 per person on the programme and £10,915 per person housed.
quote: the programme cost £10,915 per person housed per year and £7,737 per person per year on the programme.

finding: At 12 months clients significantly reduced use of homelessness and prison services, with no significant change in health service use; valued at £6,116 and £1,804 per person per year.
quote: supported clients significantly reduced their use of homelessness and prison services, though there was no significant change in use of physical or mental health services at this stage.

finding: WEMWBS wellbeing improved on all seven criteria at 6 and 12 months; annual value estimated at £6,246.
quote: This found improvements in self-reported wellbeing of participants against all seven WEMWBS criteria at 6-months and again at 12-month follow-up.

finding: Expected annual benefits (published transfer values, less 15% for negative outcomes and 30% non-additionality) £15,880 per person: public services £7,973, wellbeing £7,907.
quote: The expected annual benefits of the Housing First Pilots were estimated at £15,880 per person supported through the programme

finding: Actual annual benefits observed at 12 months, after the same adjustments, £8,429 per client: public services £4,712, wellbeing £3,716.
quote: The actual annual benefits observed at 12 months were estimated at £8,429 per Housing First client

finding: Benefit:cost ratio 2.1 (expected) and 1.1 (to date), excluding Housing Benefit; 1.6 and 0.6 if Housing Benefit deducted.
quote: This gives an expected benefit cost ratio of 2.1, and an estimated benefit: cost ratio to date of 1.1.

finding: Correction of F59 (strand Q, no transformation): internal fidelity self-assessments undertaken by two of the three Pilots (GMHF, LCRCA), not by the evaluators, are reported to score highly on separation of housing and support and an active engagement approach; no scores are given.
quote: Two of the three Pilots (GMHF and LCRCA) undertook internal fidelity self-assessments. These score highly on separation of housing and support and the use of an active engagement approach.
